Article Title: Apple Pay launches in India; here's how to set it up and where you can use it
Article Text:
Apple Pay launched in India: How it works, and who can use it

How to set up and use Apple Pay

Where you can use it

Apple has officially launched Apple Pay in India. With this launch the company brings its secure and seamless payment system to iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch users, with Mac support coming soon. Apple Pay roll out in the country will enable users to pay in stores, apps, and on the web without typing PINs and OTPs marking a significant milestone in India’s fast-growing digital payments ecosystem. At launch, Apple Pay supports Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards, enabling payments at thousands of merchants across India and anywhere NFC transactions are accepted globally.Apple also emphasised that privacy remains central to how Apple Pay functions. When a card is added, the actual card number is never stored on the device or Apple's servers, nor shared with merchants during a transaction. Instead, the system assigns a unique Device Account Number, which is encrypted and stored securely within the device's Secure Element — a certified, industry-standard chip built specifically to protect payment information.Presently, Apple Pay is exclusively available to customers holding Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards, letting them add those cards to Apple Pay and use them at thousands of in-store and online merchants across India, as well as anywhere that accepts NFC transactions.Jennifer Bailey, Apple's vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet, framed the launch as a natural fit for India's fast-growing digital economy, pointing to the country's dynamic, digitally savvy population that's increasingly embracing cashless payments while expecting strong security and privacy standards. She described Apple Pay's core value proposition as making everyday card payments easy, secure, and private — from a simple tap in stores without needing a separate app, PIN, or OTP, to checking out online without repeatedly re-entering payment details.Apple Pay is easy to set up. Customers can add a card directly to Apple Wallet via the latest version of the Axis Bank app. Alternatively, simply open the Wallet app on iPhone, tap the plus sign, and follow the steps to add an eligible card. Once a user adds a card to their Apple device, they can start using Apple Pay right away.Using Apple Pay in stores is seamless and easy. Simply double-click the side button or Home button; authenticate using Face ID, Touch ID, or a device passcode if prompted; and hold the top of the iPhone or display of the Apple Watch near the contactless reader to pay. When using Apple Pay, users will continue to earn the rewards and benefits offered by their cards.At launch, Apple Pay will be accepted at millions of merchants across India, including Apple Store locations, Blinkit, Chaayos, Comet, Croma, Interflora, Ixigo, Le15 Patisserie, Reliance brands, Tata 1mg, and Zomato, among others. Apple has also partnered with several payment service providers, including Cashfree, JusPay, Mswipe, Paytm, PayU, Pine Labs, Razorpay, and Worldline, to extend Apple Pay's reach across their respective merchant networks, with more merchants and apps expected to be added over time.Globally, Apple Pay is now available in more than 90 countries and regions, working with over 11,000 bank and network partners worldwide — making India one of the more prominent recent additions to that global rollout.
Article Summary: Apple has officially launched Apple Pay in India. The company brings its secure and seamless payment system to iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch users. Apple Pay roll out in the country will enable users to pay in stores, apps, and on the web without typing PINs and OTPs.

Article Title: Pebble launches Qore Ultra wellness band at introductory price of Rs 5,999
Article Text:
Pebble Qore Ultra

Pebble Qore Ultra features

Pebble Qore Ultra price and availability

Home-grown consumer electronics brand Pebble has launched Qore Ultra, its flagship wellness band. In a press release, the company said that the device is designed for continuous, distraction-free wear. Coming with 3 ATM water-resistant design, Qore Ultra integrates a 4-PD precision sensor array and 6-axis motion sensors. “This hardware architecture enables 24x7 tracking of vital metrics, including heart rate, HRV, SpO2, respiration, and stress, while delivering up to 15 days of continuous battery life,” it stated.The band features automatic workout detection for activities like walking and running, over 100 sports modes, and in-app GPS sports tracking. The Pebble Qore mobile application acts as the central hub for this health intelligence, seamlessly translating complex data into intuitive metrics. Users can gauge their daily preparedness through a 0-100 Readiness Score, factoring in HRV, sleep quality, and stress, while monitoring their real-time stamina via the Body Energy Score. For long-term health tracking, the platform calculates Body Age every three days and uses GPS-tracked runs to estimate VO2 Max and Fitness Age.Komal Agarwal, Co-founder of Pebble said “The Pebble Qore series has become one of India's top fitness bands, and the Qore Ultra represents the flagship evolution of that journey. We have put a significant amount of R&D into giving users actionable data that can help them improve their daily rest, activity, and habits. By providing these comprehensive insights alongside community features on our new app, we are shifting the focus from isolated tracking to shared wellness management. ”Pebble Qore Ultra will be available from October 2, 2026 in three color options, Desert Gold, Deep Black, and Deep Blue. Priced at an introductory Rs 5,999 (MRP 8,999), the wearable will be available through Pebble's official website, Flipkart, Amazon, and leading retail stores across the country.
Article Summary: Pebble Qore Ultra will be available from October 2, 2026 in three color options, Desert Gold, Deep Black, and Deep Blue. Priced at an introductory Rs 5,999 (MRP 8,999) The band features automatic workout detection for activities like walking and running, over 100 sports modes, and in-app GPS sports tracking.

Article Title: Eight trapped in lift at Kanjirappally mini civil station due to power outage
Article Text:
The lift is designed to run on battery backup during a power cut

Kottayam

:





Eight people were trapped for a while in a lift at the Kanjirappally mini civil station on Wednesday morning following a power outage. They were rescued by fire and rescue service personnel.The lift stopped between the second and third floors around 10am. Five of those trapped were employees of various departments at the station while the others were contract staff.Personnel from Kanjirappally fire and rescue station, led by station officer A Sabu, opened the lift door using a hydraulic spreader and brought all eight out.The lift is designed to run on battery backup during a power cut, moving to the nearest floor and stopping. However, the battery had not been charged, which has been cited as the reason for the stopping of the lift midway. The civil station has no diesel generator facility.
Article Summary: Eight people were trapped for a while in a lift at the Kanjirappally mini civil station on Wednesday morning. The lift is designed to run on battery backup during a power cut, moving to the nearest floor and stopping. However, the battery had not been charged, which has been cited as the reason for the stopping of the lift midway.

Article Title: After the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, scientists planted sunflowers to pull radioactive material from contaminated water and soil; the flowers actually absorbed radioactive isotopes
Article Text:
Representative image

How sunflowers absorb radioactive material after Chernobyl nuclear disaster

Chernobyl's contaminated pond experiment

Why cesium and strontium entered the plants

Why contaminated soil was much harder

Sunflowers were tested after Fukushima

What Fukushima revealed about the method

The radioactive plants had to be handled

Why water produced better results than soil

From Chernobyl to Fukushima

After the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, scientists explored an unusual way of dealing with radioactive contamination by using plants to absorb radionuclides from the environment. Sunflowers emerged as a promising candidate because their roots can take up certain radioactive elements, including cesium and strontium, from contaminated water. Experiments near Chernobyl showed that sunflowers could remove substantial amounts of radionuclides from a small contaminated pond. The approach was later investigated after the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident as well. Researchers found that the flowers could take up radioactive material, although their effectiveness varied greatly depending on whether the contamination was in water or soil.The process is known as phytoremediation, where plants are used to remove or contain pollutants. A related technique called rhizofiltration uses plant roots to capture contaminants from water. Sunflowers attracted attention because they grow rapidly, produce substantial biomass and absorb elements through their normal nutrient-uptake processes. Radioactive cesium-137 has chemical similarities to potassium, an essential plant nutrient, while strontium-90 behaves in some ways like calcium.These similarities allow plants to take up radioactive forms of the elements through pathways used for nutrients, making sunflowers a useful candidate for experiments involving contaminated water and soil.One of the best-known demonstrations was carried out in the Chernobyl area using a small contaminated pond. Rather than simply planting sunflowers in the surrounding soil, researchers grew them on floating rafts placed in the water, allowing their roots to extend into the contaminated pond. A US Environmental Protection Agency technology assessment reported that sunflowers used in the Chernobyl demonstration extracted about 95% of the radionuclides from the pond within 10 days. The experiment involved rhizofiltration and focused on radioactive cesium and strontium. The result demonstrated that plants could capture significant quantities of radioactive material when the contaminants were accessible in water.The uptake of radioactive isotopes by plants is closely connected to their chemistry. Cesium-137 has similarities to potassium, which plants need for normal growth, meaning radioactive cesium can enter through some of the same biological pathways used to absorb potassium. Strontium-90 is chemically similar to calcium, allowing plants to absorb it through processes associated with calcium uptake. Once absorbed, the radionuclides can move through the plant and accumulate in different tissues, including roots, stems and leaves. The amount and location of accumulation depend on the isotope, plant species and growing conditions. The process transfers radioactive material into the plant rather than destroying the radioactivity itself.The impressive results from contaminated water did not automatically translate to radioactive soil. Cesium can become strongly attached to soil particles, particularly clay minerals, making it much less mobile and less available to plant roots. Japan's Ministry of the Environment explains that minerals including vermiculite and illite can strongly fix radioactive cesium in soil, reducing the amount that can dissolve into soil water and subsequently enter plants. This became particularly important after Fukushima, where radiocesium contaminated large areas of agricultural land. The amount of cesium present in soil therefore did not necessarily correspond to the amount that a sunflower could absorb.The sunflower approach was also investigated following the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident. Japanese researchers tested several plants to determine whether they could absorb radiocesium from contaminated agricultural soil, with sunflowers among the species examined. A Japanese government report describes a demonstration in Iitate Village, where sunflowers and other plants were grown in soil containing approximately 7,715 becquerels of radiocesium per kilogram. Researchers measured the amount of radiocesium taken up by the plants and examined the resulting plant material. The trials formed part of wider research into whether phytoremediation could provide an alternative method for dealing with contaminated farmland.The Fukushima experiments showed that a plant's ability to absorb cesium does not necessarily mean it can remove enough cesium from soil to make large-scale decontamination practical. The problem was largely connected to the way cesium interacted with the soil. After radioactive cesium reaches clay-rich soil, it can become strongly fixed to mineral surfaces, remaining concentrated near the surface while becoming increasingly unavailable to plant roots. Scientific studies of Fukushima soils have found that weathered mica and other minerals can strongly bind Cs-137, reducing its transfer from soil into vegetation. Consequently, sunflower cultivation alone could not extract enough radioactive cesium from contaminated agricultural soil to serve as a comprehensive decontamination method.When sunflowers absorb radionuclides, the radioactive material becomes concentrated in their tissues, meaning harvesting the plants does not eliminate the radioactivity. Instead, it transfers part of the contamination into plant biomass that must be collected and appropriately managed. This is a central part of phytoremediation: the plant acts as a biological collector, taking contaminants out of water or soil and concentrating them in a smaller quantity of material. In the Chernobyl water experiments, this made it possible to repeatedly use plants to capture radionuclides from contaminated water before removing the resulting biomass from the environment.The difference between the two environments comes down largely to the availability of the radioactive material. Radionuclides dissolved or suspended in water can come into direct contact with plant roots, allowing the roots to absorb them more readily. Soil is more complicated because contaminants can become attached to mineral particles, trapped within soil structures or otherwise become unavailable to plants. This helps explain why the Chernobyl pond experiment produced striking results while attempts to remove radioactive cesium from soil were considerably more difficult. The effectiveness of phytoremediation therefore depends not only on the plant but also on the chemical and physical conditions surrounding its roots.The experiments following the two nuclear disasters helped scientists better understand the potential and limitations of plant-based radioactive cleanup. At Chernobyl, sunflowers demonstrated that plant roots could capture radionuclides from contaminated water, while at Fukushima researchers tested whether the same biological mechanism could help remove radioactive cesium from agricultural soil. The results showed that the surrounding chemistry was as important as the plant itself. Sunflowers could absorb radioactive isotopes, but the amount they could remove depended on how easily those isotopes could move from the environment into the roots. Their ability to capture cesium and strontium consequently made them a useful subject for phytoremediation research, even though the approach could not by itself provide a large-scale solution for contaminated soil.
Article Summary: After the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, scientists explored an unusual way of dealing with radioactive contamination by using plants. Sunflowers emerged as a promising candidate because their roots can take up certain radioactive elements, including cesium and strontium, from contaminated water. Experiments near Chernobyl showed that sunflowers could remove substantial amounts of radionuclides from a small contaminated pond. The approach was later investigated after the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident as well.

Article Title: Meet Serge Boghossian, the 16-year-old Canadian student who taught himself to code and built a job platform; hundreds of teens have already joined
Article Text:
Serge Boghossian. Image Credit: INSAUGA Mississauga/Website

Serge Boghossian from Canada build a job platform for teenagers

Image Credit: Modern Mississauga/Website

Need of a separate platform for young job seekers

Image Credit: Modern Mississauga

Challenges faced by Serge while developing Jobbli

How does Jobbli handle the needs of teenage users

What happened after the first version was released

How Boghossian plans to expand Jobbli

16-year-old Serge Boghossian has turned a problem he faced while looking for work into a platform designed to help other teenagers find their first jobs. The Mississauga student taught himself to code and built Jobbli, a free online service connecting local teenagers with businesses offering part-time work. The idea came from seeing friends struggle to find employment and from his own difficulty getting a first opportunity. What began as a small project has since developed into a platform that Boghossian hopes can eventually reach young job seekers beyond his home city.Boghossian was born and raised in Mississauga and began working on Jobbli after noticing how difficult it could be for teenagers to enter the job market. Modern Mississauga reported that the idea came to him in November 2025 after watching friends struggle to find their first jobs. He spent about 2 weeks researching and planning before writing his first line of code.The rest of the process was largely self-directed. According to The Pointer, Boghossian had no mentor or school programme teaching him how to code, and he did not rely on his parents to build the platform. Instead, he learnt through YouTube tutorials and continued working on his skills until he could create the service himself.Before Jobbli, he had already built a messaging platform using HTML and JavaScript. That earlier project gave him experience that he later used to create the more complex job platform, The Pointer reported.Jobbli was created around a straightforward gap in the employment market. Modern Mississauga described it as a free, local platform for Mississauga teenagers aged 14 to 17 who are looking for part-time work. The publication reported that many mainstream job sites are designed with adults in mind, while listings suitable for younger workers can be scattered across social media, word of mouth and community noticeboards.Boghossian also noticed that local businesses faced the opposite problem. Restaurants, tutoring centres, banquet halls and gyms could be interested in hiring teenagers but did not always have an easy way to reach them. Jobbli was designed to bring both sides together in one place.The Pointer reported that Boghossian wanted the platform to be easy for teenagers to use, instead of expecting them to have professional qualifications or years of experience. Teens can look for opportunities, apply and communicate with employers through the platform.Creating the technology was only part of the challenge. Modern Mississauga reported that Boghossian found being taken seriously at 16 difficult, particularly when speaking directly with restaurant owners and local organisations. He had to demonstrate that the project was more than a school experiment.The business side also required him to learn skills that were not part of coding. He had to work out how to approach employers, explain the idea and follow up when businesses did not respond positively. Building the platform alone also meant spending long hours fixing problems in his own code without a senior developer to turn to, according to Modern Mississauga.His first step towards wider local recognition came when he contacted the Cooksville Business Improvement Area(BIA) himself. The Pointer reported that he cold-called the organisation to ask whether it could help promote Jobbli and later met with the BIA in person.Because the platform is intended for teenagers, Boghossian has placed particular attention on privacy and safety. The Pointer reported that Jobbli uses Supabase for built-in security features, including measures intended to reduce the risk of employers sending harmful links to young job seekers.That concern is particularly important because the platform deals with minors. Boghossian said the privacy layer was intended to make teenagers less vulnerable while communicating with employers.Modern Mississauga also reported that employers can post jobs for free, while teenagers can apply, message employers and arrange interviews through the same platform. The aim is to make the process less scattered than the traditional search for a first job.Boghossian did not wait until Jobbli was completely polished before allowing people to use it. The Pointer reported that he released Version 1.0 to gather feedback and see whether teenagers would engage with the idea.That early release helped him improve the platform before trying to reach a wider audience. Modern Mississauga reported that his first version was not perfect, but getting it into the hands of real users allowed him to begin conversations with employers rather than continuing to work on it privately.The response from teenagers and parents was described as particularly encouraging as per Modern Mississauga, although Boghossian said employers needed more convincing before trying something new. The Pointer reported that he was also in early discussions with myBlueprint, a Canadian education and career planning platform used by students and parents.For now, the focus remains on Mississauga. The Pointer reported that Boghossian's immediate task is to persuade more local employers to use the platform while attracting teenagers to it. Modern Mississauga reported that Boghossian wants other young entrepreneurs to build something for a community they understand personally. His own experience as a Mississauga teenager helped him recognise a problem among people his age and shape a tool around it.
Article Summary: Serge Boghossian from Canada built a job platform for teenagers. The Mississauga student taught himself to code and built Jobbli. It is a free online service connecting local teenagers with businesses offering part-time work. Teens can look for opportunities, apply and communicate with employers.

Article Title: In 2002, Scotland opened the Falkirk Wheel to lift boats 100 feet between canals, replacing 11 locks with a rotating 1,800-tonne structure
Article Text:
PC: Wikipedia

How the Falkirk Wheel replaced 11 locks with a rotating boat lift

How the Falkirk Wheel raises boats 100 feet between two Scottish canals

PC: Wikipedia

How the Falkirk Wheel uses 1.5 kWh to rotate its 1,800-tonne structure

How the Falkirk Wheel cut a full-day canal journey to just a few minutes

Opened in 2002, the Falkirk Wheel transformed how boats travel between two historic canals in central Scotland. The rotating boat lift connects the Forth and Clyde Canal with the Union Canal, which lies about 100 feet higher. Instead of relying on the former flight of 11 locks, the structure uses two water-filled gondolas that rotate to raise and lower vessels. The system was designed to keep the gondolas balanced, allowing the 1,800-tonne structure to operate using just 1.5 kWh for each rotation, according to Scottish Canals. The energy used is commonly compared with that required to boil eight kettles. Beyond its engineering brilliance, the Falkirk Wheel has become a beloved Scottish landmark, proving that thoughtfully restored waterways can unite heritage, innovation, and tourism while inviting half a million visitors annually to marvel at Archimedes' principle in action.The Falkirk Wheel was built as part of efforts to restore the Forth and Clyde Canal and the Union Canal. The Forth and Clyde Canal was built in 1790, while the Union Canal opened in 1822. The two waterways had originally been connected at Falkirk through a series of 11 locks, but the locks later became unusable, and the canals were eventually closed.The restoration project sought a new way to connect the waterways rather than simply rebuilding the old staircase of locks.The Linda Hall Library says British Waterways Scotland worked with architectural and engineering firms to develop a unique boat-lift design. The resulting structure uses two gondolas positioned on opposite sides of the rotating wheel, allowing boats to be raised and lowered as the wheel turns.Each side of the Falkirk Wheel contains a gondola capable of carrying canal boats. The Linda Hall Library states that each gondola can accommodate up to four canal boats, or one or two larger boats. Once the boats enter, seals are raised to make the gondolas watertight, and the wheel rotates to exchange their positions. Scottish Canals similarly describes the Wheel as connecting the two canals 35 metres above.A central feature of the design is the balance between the two gondolas. The two gondolas, when full of water, weigh the same regardless of how many boats they contain. It attributes this to Archimedes’ principle: when a boat enters a full gondola, it displaces water equal to its own weight, leaving the total weight unchanged.According to Scottish Canals, the structure weighs 1,800 tonnes and uses just 1.5 kWh for each rotation. The Linda Hall Library gives a figure of about 1.5 kilowatt-hours for one half-turn and notes the commonly cited comparison that this is about the same amount of energy required to boil eight kettles of water.Before the Wheel was built, vessels travelling between the two canals had to pass through the former flight of 11 locks. Scottish Canals says this meant opening and closing 44 lock gates and could take a full day. The Wheel reduced the canal transfer to a journey of only a few minutes. The rotating lift therefore replaced a lengthy sequence of lock operations with a single mechanical movement, dramatically reducing the time needed for boats to change canals. The new connection also restored a navigable link between the two historic waterways, helping bring the canals back into regular use after decades of closure.Since opening, the Falkirk Wheel has also become a major visitor destination. Scottish Canals says it attracts around 500,000 visitors each year and describes it as one of Scotland's busiest tourist attractions. The organisation calls it a "working sculpture" combining modern engineering and technology with principles associated with Archimedes.
Article Summary: The Falkirk Wheel was built in 2002 to connect the Forth and Clyde Canal and the Union Canal in central Scotland. Instead of relying on the former flight of 11 locks, the structure uses two water-filled gondolas that rotate to raise and lower vessels. The 1,800-tonne structure uses just 1.5 kWh for each rotation.

Article Title: London designer turns waste mussel shells and local Thames sand into glass; wins £10,000 Design Museum prize
Article Text:
Representative Image of a designer creating glass objects using quagga mussel shells and local materials from the River Thames (AI Generated Image)

Quagga mussel shells became one of the key ingredients

Thames Glass grew from a collaboration with Thames Water

The material has also been tested as architectural cladding

The prize will support Harrison's next stage of research

London designer Lulu Harrison has won the 2025 Ralph Saltzman Prize from the Design Museum for Thames Glass, a project that turns locally sourced and waste materials into glass. Harrison's recipes use materials including sand from around the River Thames, wood ash and waste quagga mussel shells supplied by Thames Water. The Design Museum describes Harrison as a geo-alchemist glass artist whose project explores the possibility of creating geo-specific glass from abundant and waste materials associated with a particular place. Harrison was selected as the fourth recipient of the annual prize by a jury comprising industrial designer Konstantin Grcic, material designer Seetal Solanki, artist and designer Stephen Burks and design journalist and author Michelle Ogundehin, alongside Lisa Saltzman. The judges praised Harrison's research and her approach to mapping the raw materials used in the glass and communicating that process to audiences. She received a £10,000 bursary to continue developing her work. This innovative project demonstrates how creative material science can transform environmental waste streams into artistic and functional applications, offering promising possibilities for sustainable design innovation.A central component of Thames Glass is the shell of the quagga mussel, an invasive non-native species that can cause blockages in Thames Water's transfer tunnels and has to be removed. Harrison says her collaboration with Thames Water gave her access to the waste shells, which would otherwise require disposal. She combines ground-up mussel shells with local sand and waste wood ash to create different glass recipes. Her own project description says the work began with experiments using local and waste materials sourced in and around the Thames, including waste shells from water companies and wood ash or bracken from surrounding forests. The resulting glass has been used to create objects including carafes, tumblers and other vessels, with the material's natural impurities contributing to its distinctive appearance. Harrison developed the project while studying for an MA in Material Futures at Central Saint Martins and has worked with glassblowers, glass chemists and glass archaeologists during its development.The project developed through Harrison's work with Thames Water while she was studying at Central Saint Martins. Harrison has said that the collaboration helped her find a use for the tonnes of quagga mussel shells being removed because the animals were blocking water infrastructure. Her early work produced prototypes of a Thames Glass carafe and tumbler, while later experiments explored other forms and applications. Central Saint Martins documented the project in 2022, describing Harrison's use of local sands, waste shells and wood ash and her collaboration with Thames Water. Harrison has also worked with Here Design, glassblowers and other specialists to develop the material and its applications. Rather than presenting Thames Glass as a replacement for conventional glass, Harrison describes the project as an exploration of alternative glassmaking recipes based on materials associated with a particular geographical area.Harrison later worked with London architecture studio Bureau de Change to investigate whether Thames Glass could be used on buildings. The collaboration produced a series of cast glass façade tiles made using the material, with patterns inspired by London's architectural history, including designs found on 19th-century terracotta chimney pots. The tiles were presented as part of Beautility: How Fusing Beauty and Function Can Change the World, an exhibition curated by Here Design during London Craft Week. Bureau de Change says the project explored whether Thames Glass could be used as an alternative material for building cladding, while Harrison's own project page describes the tiles as an exploration of future applications for the material. The collaboration therefore moved Thames Glass beyond vessels and into architectural experimentation, although the work remains a design and material research project rather than an established commercial building product.The Ralph Saltzman Prize gives Harrison £10,000 to continue developing Thames Glass and provides an opportunity to display the project at the Design Museum. The museum describes the prize as an annual award for emerging product designers whose practices explore new directions in design, including technical innovation, sustainability and cultural re-evaluation. Harrison's 2025 project was displayed at the museum from June 24 to August 25, 2025. In describing the award, Harrison said her practice is driven by research, process, collaboration, experimentation and hands-on making, connecting craft and science while exploring more localised possibilities for glassmaking. Thames Glass is still fundamentally an experimental material project, but its use of waste quagga mussel shells, local sand and waste ash demonstrates how materials removed from one system can become ingredients in another.
Article Summary: London designer Lulu Harrison has won the 2025 Ralph Saltzman Prize for Thames Glass. The project uses locally sourced and waste materials to create glass. Harrison's recipes use materials including sand from around the River Thames, wood ash and waste quagga mussel shells supplied by Thames Water. The prize will support Harrison's next stage of research.

Article Title: Bentley launches first fully electric Torcal in 107-year history at £173,000, undercutting Ferrari Luce with 375-mile range and 10-80% charging in under 20 minutes
Article Text:
Bentley has launched the Torcal, its first fully electric vehicle in 107 years. (Photo: Bentley)

Bentley says wealthy buyers are increasingly accepting EVs

Torcal specifications in detail

The Bentley Torcal offers a driving range of up to 375 miles. (Photo: Bentley)

New Bentley design language debuts with the Torcal

Bentley has combined electric performance with its signature luxury design and handcrafted cabin. (Photo: Bentley)

Cabin combines leather, wood, wool and aluminium with digital technology

The Bentley Torcal starts at £173,000, significantly below Ferrari’s Luce EV. (Photo: Bentley)

Four Experience modes change the character of the car

Bentley recreates engine character for its electric SUV

S version brings a more aggressive exterior

Bentley wants the Torcal to remain a Bentley first

British luxury carmaker Bentley Motors has entered the electric vehicle market with the launch of the all-new Torcal, its first fully electric model in the company’s 107-year history. The new electric SUV marks a significant step for Bentley as the luxury automotive industry continues to test the appetite of affluent buyers for high-performance EVs.The Torcal, which was unveiled in London on Wednesday evening, becomes the fourth model in Bentley’s current line-up alongside the Continental GT, Flying Spur and Bentayga. Designed and engineered at Bentley’s headquarters in Crewe, northwest England, the electric SUV has been developed to combine the brand’s traditional craftsmanship with new electric technology, performance and a completely new design language.The Torcal starts at £173,000, or around $229,000, placing it substantially below Ferrari’s first electric vehicle, the Luce, which carries a reported starting price of around €550,000 ($626,000). Ferrari launched the Luce three months before Bentley’s EV, with its design drawing mixed reactions from some observers and analysts.Speaking to CNBC’s Squawk Box Europe, Bentley Motors chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser said the Torcal sits at the entry level of Bentley’s price range and has received positive reactions across markets.Walliser said Bentley was not looking at Ferrari’s Luce launch for lessons because the development of a luxury vehicle is a long-term process. He pointed out that Bentley works on a roughly four-year development cycle and cannot change direction simply in response to what another manufacturer has launched.According to Walliser, acceptance of electric cars among Bentley’s wealthy clientele is continuing to grow, with customers becoming increasingly knowledgeable about EV technology.The comments come as several luxury manufacturers reassess their electric strategies. Porsche and Lamborghini, for instance, have scaled back aspects of their EV plans amid weaker-than-expected demand in parts of the luxury electric-car market.Bentley’s approach with the Torcal has been to make the vehicle feel like a Bentley first, regardless of its powertrain. The company says particular attention has been paid to design, driving behaviour, sound and the overall sensory experience.The Torcal is a five-metre-long electric SUV and is the shortest four-door Bentley yet produced. It has a wheelbase designed to maximise cabin space while its short overhangs, long bonnet and upright front end give it the powerful stance Bentley wanted for its new design direction.The electric SUV offers a driving range of up to 375 miles, or approximately 600 km, depending on specification and conditions. Bentley says the vehicle can charge from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes when connected to a 400kW charging system. The company also says around 100 miles of range can be added in seven minutes.Two versions will be available at launch: the Core and the S.The Core version develops 810bhp and 1,194Nm of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in 3.3 seconds and has a top speed of 155mph.The more performance-focused S produces 876bhp and up to 1,350Nm of torque with Launch Control. It can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in just 2.8 seconds, while its top speed rises to 162mph.Bentley says the electric powertrain allows the Torcal to combine supercar-like acceleration with what it describes as year-round usability.The vehicle provides 460 litres of boot space, while a further 90-litre front luggage compartment is available under the bonnet. Its turning circle is 11.1 metres, an important consideration for a vehicle measuring around five metres in length.The Torcal represents the production interpretation of Bentley’s EXP 15 concept, which was first revealed in 2025. Its design introduces a new visual direction for the marque while retaining elements intended to connect the electric SUV with Bentley’s heritage.Lead designer Robin Page describes the design process through four key areas: proportion, graphical elements, surface language and detail.The long wheelbase, short overhangs, long bonnet and upright front create what Bentley calls a “powerful stance” and “upright elegance”. The company says the proportions are intended to make the Torcal immediately recognisable as a Bentley despite its new electric architecture.The front features an illuminated diamond grille and advanced lighting elements. The rear graphics form what Bentley describes as a prestigious shield, while several design cues reference the EXP 15 concept and historic Bentley models, including the Continental T.Rather than relying on numerous character lines, Bentley has used a more sculptural approach. The surfaces taper towards the rear, creating what the company describes as the appearance of a “resting beast”.The diamond pattern seen on the exterior continues into the cabin, creating a visual link between the outside and inside of the vehicle.Inside, the Torcal blends traditional Bentley materials with modern technology.The dashboard takes inspiration from a wing and combines leather, wood or veneer and aluminium. Bentley has retained physical controls in key areas, including the centre console and steering wheel, while curved OLED displays provide the main digital interface.The seats offer 16-way adjustment, along with heating, ventilation, adjustable bolsters and massage functions. Optional postural adjustment and smart climate functions are also available.A wellness-focused seat function can provide leg massage, adding another element to Bentley’s emphasis on long-distance comfort.The company has also placed considerable emphasis on sustainable material choices. The cabin can use leather, wood, wool and aluminium, including what Bentley describes as the world’s first 100% Merino wool automotive fabric, which is certified by the Responsible Wool Standard.Sustainably sourced walnut offcuts are also used in the interior.For additional practicality, Bentley has introduced power-folding rear seats for the first time in the model.The Torcal features four Experience modes that alter various aspects of the vehicle, including lighting, sound, climate, airflow and the amount of digital information presented to the driver.Comfort mode is designed around a calmer environment and a more relaxed experience, including what Bentley describes as a digital detox approach.Sport mode, meanwhile, increases the intensity of the experience with a more immersive soundtrack and changes to the lighting and other cabin elements.Facial-recognition technology can also identify individual occupants and automatically adjust settings such as the seat, steering wheel and certain advanced driver-assistance system preferences.The Torcal uses a network of 25 radars, sensors and cameras to support its driver-assistance and vehicle-monitoring systems.One of the more distinctive aspects of the Torcal is its approach to sound.Instead of leaving the cabin silent, Bentley has created the Bentley Dynamic Symphony, an artificial soundtrack designed around the rhythms and character associated with the company’s historic combustion engines.The sound incorporates elements inspired by Bentley’s 6¾-litre V8, combined with drums, viola and bass guitar.The soundtrack is calibrated to the vehicle’s torque demand and speed, with the intensity, volume and feedback increasing when the driver selects Sport mode.Bentley has also developed a more advanced audio system for the cabin. The standard system produces 620 watts through 16 speakers, while the optional system delivers 1,780 watts through 28 speakers with Dolby Atmos. The upgraded system also incorporates kinaesthetic seat shakers and speakers positioned in the front headrests.The Torcal S receives additional styling changes to distinguish it from the Core version.These include black exterior brightware, black mirror caps, darker rear lamps, rear diffusers and sportier side sills. The front bumper also receives additional strakes, while red brake calipers add another performance-oriented visual element.Inside, the S introduces its own colour split, quilting and stitching treatments.While the S offers the highest output at 876bhp, Bentley says the focus is not simply on outright acceleration. The company has attempted to combine the additional performance with the comfort, refinement and usability traditionally associated with its luxury grand tourers and SUVs.The Torcal arrives at a critical point for the luxury EV market, where manufacturers are balancing increasingly powerful electric drivetrains with changing customer expectations.Bentley’s first fully electric model was originally expected to arrive earlier, but its launch was pushed back amid softer demand for luxury electric vehicles.The company is now betting that its established design language, handcrafted interior, high performance and focus on sound and sensory experience can make the transition to electric power feel familiar to existing Bentley customers.With a starting price of £173,000, a range of up to 375 miles, charging from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes and as much as 876bhp in S specification, the Torcal represents Bentley’s attempt to bring electric propulsion into its traditional luxury performance formula.The model is expected to go on sale by the end of the year, although the extensive range of available options can push the final price significantly higher.
Article Summary: Bentley Torcal is first fully electric model in the company's 107-year history. It starts at £173,000, significantly below Ferrari’s Luce EV. The Torcal offers a driving range of up to 375 miles and can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in 3.3 seconds.

Article Title: A retired UK rail engineer turned his East Sussex garden into a working railway using a Victorian platelayer’s trolley; the line now runs 50 feet and uses a 12-volt battery charged by solar power
Article Text:
During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex (Image Credit: George Carden/BBC)

From railway career to garden railway

A 50-foot railway in the garden

Backshall's garden contains a collection of authentic railway-related objects, including signs, signals and other equipment (Image Credit: George Carden/BBC)

From hand power to solar energy

Railway memorabilia fills the garden

A lockdown project that kept growing

A former railway engineer has transformed his garden in East Sussex into an unusual working railway, complete with full-size track, a vintage-style carriage and railway memorabilia. Railway Magazine, which featured Adrian Backshall’s project, describes the 50-foot line as a Wickham lookalike built on an old platelayer’s trolley. The small railway now uses a 12-volt car battery charged by a solar panel to power its winch, allowing the carriage to travel slowly along the garden track. What began as a lockdown project has since grown into a distinctive railway-themed garden attraction for Backshall, his family and guests.Adrian Backshall retired from Network Rail in 2018 after a career working on Britain's railways. His connection with railway equipment, however, did not end with retirement. During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex. The project gave him a way to put his railway knowledge and collection of equipment to use while spending more time at home.The centrepiece is a carriage based on a Victorian platelayer's trolley. A friend who was a blacksmith helped create the Wickham-style body that sits on top of the original trolley.Platelayers' trolleys were lightweight railway vehicles historically used by railway workers to travel along tracks while carrying tools and equipment. Backshall's version retains the character of such a vehicle while giving it a new purpose as a garden railway carriage.What started as a much shorter line has now become a 50-foot railway running through the garden. Some of the track used in the project dates back to 1898, giving the otherwise modern garden installation a genuine connection with railway history. Backshall has also added railway signs, signals and other pieces of equipment around the property, making the garden resemble a miniature railway museum.The railway has two main stopping points, near the garden shed and patio. The line is not designed for speed. Instead, the carriage moves slowly enough for passengers to enjoy the unusual surroundings as it makes its journey through the garden. According to Railway Magazine, the 50-foot cable-worked railway has a maximum speed of about 0.3 miles per hour. That extremely slow pace is part of the charm of the project. Rather than trying to recreate a conventional railway journey, Backshall has created something closer to a moving garden room with a genuine railway feel.The railway has also evolved technically since its early days. Initially, the carriage was moved using a hand-cranked pulley arrangement. As the project expanded, Backshall replaced that system with a 12-volt winch. The winch is powered by a 12-volt car battery, which is charged using a solar panel. This allows the railway to operate without relying on a conventional mains-powered system for its movement.The arrangement combines old railway equipment with simple modern technology. A Victorian-era trolley forms the basis of the carriage, while solar power provides the energy needed to move it along the track. The result is a small but functioning railway that reflects Backshall's interest in both railway history and engineering.The track is only part of the transformation. Backshall's garden contains a collection of authentic railway-related objects, including signs, signals and other equipment. Some of the signs retain the language associated with working railway lines, giving visitors the impression that they have stepped into a small railway installation rather than an ordinary residential garden.Inside the carriage, the railway theme continues. The cabin has seating for four people and includes a wood-burning stove, while railway memorabilia and other details make the space suitable for entertaining. Backshall and his wife Ruth have used the train for gatherings and tea parties, turning the unusual railway into part of their home life. The project has also involved some negotiation over space. As the railway was extended, the track passed through part of the garden that had previously been used for flowers. Ruth has spoken about the changes with humour, while supporting the project that began as a lockdown idea.Backshall's railway demonstrates how a small hobby can develop into a much more elaborate personal project. The original lockdown railway was considerably shorter, but the line has since been extended to 50 feet. The addition of a solar-powered winch has also made the operation more convenient than the original hand-powered arrangement. For someone who spent decades around Britain's railways, the project offers a way to preserve that connection after retirement. Instead of simply displaying an old trolley, Backshall has incorporated it into a functioning railway environment. The garden railway has also attracted wider attention. Backshall and Ruth held an open day in June 2025 to raise money for St Wilfrid's Hospice, allowing the unusual project to serve a charitable purpose as well.Today, the 50-foot line stands as an unusual combination of railway history, engineering and gardening. With its Victorian trolley, historic track, railway signs and solar-powered 12-volt system, Backshall's creation has turned an ordinary East Sussex garden into a working piece of railway heritage.
Article Summary: Adrian Backshall retired from Network Rail in 2018 after a career working on Britain's railways. During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex. The railway now uses a 12-volt car battery charged by a solar panel to power its winch, allowing the carriage to travel slowly along the track.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Radisson Blu Palace Resort & Spa, Udaipur adds a touch of luxury to the mix, allowing travellers to combine wellness, culture and leisure in one short stay.Because sometimes, you don't need a week-long holiday to feel refreshed. You just need a change of view, a little less screen time and a couple of days that are entirely your own.

Article Title: From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape
Article Text:
From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape

Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.

From discarded tyres to footwear with a purpose, the idea began with a childhood experience. At the age of 10, UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar visited rural Africa, where he saw children walking long distances barefoot, often without adequate footwear.Moved by what he witnessed, Ahaan gave away his favourite pair of slippers to a child he met during the visit. The experience stayed with him long after he returned home and eventually became the starting point for a larger idea.As he grew older, Ahaan began exploring how discarded materials could be repurposed to address the lack of affordable, durable footwear. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles.The idea brought together two concerns he had encountered separately: the growing problem of tyre waste and the need for accessible footwear.He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala, and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day. Ahaan then connected with Mamco General Trading, which operates in Uganda and Zambia. As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility programme, the company will purchase 4,000 pairs of slippers each month for free distribution to children and families in need. It’s a sustainable cycle that turns waste into opportunity, supporting livelihoods and giving kids durable footwear.“When I was 10 years old, I saw children my age walking barefoot, and I never forgot that moment,” Ahaan says. “I wanted to create something that could help people and the environment. If we can turn discarded tyres into something useful and long-lasting, maybe it can inspire more young people to believe their simple ideas can really make a difference.”The world’s growing dependence on convenience and mobility comes with an environmental cost. Every year, more than a billion tyres reach the end of their usable life, creating a significant waste-management challenge. Many of these tyres end up in landfills, while others are burned or processed in ways that can contribute to pollution and the loss of valuable materials.Repurposing discarded tyres offers one way to address this challenge by keeping materials in use for longer and reducing the amount of waste that needs to be disposed of. Turning old tyres into durable slipper soles, for instance, gives a material that would otherwise be discarded a new application while also reducing the need for virgin raw materials in footwear production.The approach reflects a broader shift in how sustainability is being understood. Rather than treating waste simply as something to be collected and discarded, initiatives like this explore how materials already in circulation can be redesigned and put to practical use.In doing so, they can support waste reduction, resource conservation and efforts to lower the environmental impact associated with new production. Ultimately, sustainability is not only about recycling what has already been used, but also about rethinking waste as a potential resource.
Article Summary: UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar saw children walking barefoot in rural Africa. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles. He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day.

Article Title: Bill Gates does not agree with possibility of AI Kill Switch; says: It's not enough to have a Kill Switch, they're not yet at the point where...
Article Text:
Bill Gates dismissed the idea as somewhat misguided

The real danger, in his view: bad actors, not rogue AI

Self-regulation isn't enough, Bill Gates says

On the AI safety whistleblower and existential risk

Bill Gates warns AI risks are real, but not a hoax

Microsoft founder Bill Gates has pushed back against the growing calls for an AI ‘Kill Switch’, arguing that the discussion misses the more immediate dangers posed by artificial intelligence and reflects a misunderstanding of how current systems operate. Speaking in an interview with NBC News, Gates said AI systems remain under human control and are not yet capable of autonomously taking over computer networks or operating independently without oversight. “The kill switches, that's kind of a weird thing. It's not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates said. “They're not yet at the point where they autonomously grab computers and can't be shut down.” Rather than relying on emergency shutdown mechanisms, Gates argued that governments and industry should prioritise monitoring systems and safeguards that can detect misuse of advanced AI models.Asked directly whether an AI kill switch is realistic, Gates dismissed the idea as somewhat misguided, arguing that AI systems aren't yet autonomous enough to seize control of computers in a way that would make shutting them down difficult in the first place. He said the entire framing of the debate reveals how little technical understanding many people bring to the conversation, and made clear he wasn't opposed to a kill switch outright — but stressed that moderating bad behavior really requires ongoing insight and records of what a system is actually doing, something a kill switch alone can't provide.Gates was direct in saying he doesn't believe AI has slipped out of human control, noting that these systems aren't yet operating millions of robots and that humans retain the ability to simply turn off the underlying computers. The more urgent threat, he argued, comes from people with malicious intent using AI to defraud individuals, disable electrical grids, or disrupt banking systems — capabilities that historically required the resources of a nation-state but are now within reach of small groups thanks to AI.He pointed to Anthropic's own reporting on people attempting to use its AI to help design bioweapons or targeting systems as evidence that these risks are already materializing, not hypothetical. Gates said AI has effectively made sophisticated fraud radically more accessible, arguing that scammers no longer need manual effort when AI can perform the task far more convincingly and at far greater scale.Pressed on whether the industry can be trusted to police itself, Gates was unambiguous: self-regulation is not sufficient, and legislation out of Washington is needed. He argued that lawmakers and law enforcement need to be directly involved in defining what safeguards and monitoring should look like, framing it as a mandatory requirement rather than a voluntary best practice — while maintaining that implementing these safeguards wouldn't meaningfully slow down AI development.He also drew a sharp distinction between the near-term risks he sees as urgent and the more distant, headline-grabbing fear of AI escaping human control entirely. While he called that longer-term risk worth taking seriously, he said the real and present danger today comes from humans misusing AI, not AI acting entirely on its own.Referencing a recent industry whistleblower's warning that AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade, Gates said AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events capable of causing a billion deaths, calling the combination of AI tools and people with harmful intent an unprecedented kind of danger. He welcomed the fact that people within the industry are now speaking openly about these risks, even against their own commercial interests, but expressed concern that much of the wider world is either dismissing the warnings or treating AI purely as a competitive race rather than a shared problem requiring coordinated thinking.Gates also rejected claims that warnings about AI-related existential risks are exaggerated.“It's not a hoax at all,” he said, while noting that current concerns should focus on preventing misuse before catastrophic incidents occur.The remarks come as debate intensifies across the AI industry over regulation, model safety and the balance between rapid technological progress and risk management. Gates said advanced AI systems have already crossed important thresholds in areas such as cybersecurity and biological research, making the introduction of safeguards an urgent priority.At the same time, he maintained that AI remains one of the most transformative technologies ever created, with the potential to improve healthcare, education and scientific research if developed responsibly.
Article Summary: Bill Gates has pushed back against the growing calls for an AI ‘Kill Switch’ He argued that the discussion misses the more immediate dangers posed by artificial intelligence and reflects a misunderstanding of how current systems operate. Gates said the real and present danger today comes from humans misusing AI, not AI acting entirely on its own.
