Article Title: Starting October 1, WhatsApp to 'stop' delivering messages from these WhatsApp Business accounts
Article Text:
Which WhatsApp Business accounts will be affected

Why is Meta charging for WhatsApp Business messages

How will service messages be charged

What happens if a business does not add a payment method

How WhatsApp Business charges will work from October 1

​WhatsApp Business users could see their messages stop being delivered from October 1 if their accounts do not have a payment method on file. Meta is introducing per-message charges for service messages starting today, ending a period when these messages were not charged. As part of the change, Meta has warned Solution Providers and businesses using direct integrations that it will stop delivering service messages for accounts that have not added a payment method by September 30.In a blog post, the company wrote, “For any Solution Provider or directly-integrated businesses that does not have a payment method on file by September 30, 2026, Meta will stop delivering service messages as of when they become charged on October 1, 2026.” The change applies to non-template service messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window.The change applies to Solution Providers and businesses that directly integrate with the WhatsApp Business Platform. Businesses in these categories need to have a payment method associated with their messaging accounts by September 30 to avoid service-message delivery being stopped from October 1.Service messages are non-template messages powered by a customer service representative or a third-party AI solution. They are different from messages powered by Meta Business Agent, which became a separate category in July 2026.Meta says it is introducing the changes as part of its H2 2026 pricing updates. Service messages will be charged per message starting October 1, and utility messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window will also become chargeable that day.Service messages have not been charged since November 1, 2024, while the specific utility messages covered by the change have been free since July 1, 2025.Meta will charge for delivered service messages rather than simply messages sent by businesses. The charge will be calculated per message, with rates varying by market.The company says service-message rates will match its utility and authentication message rates in each market. There will also be no volume tiers for service messages.Businesses can send non-template messages only while a 24-hour customer service window is open. That window opens or resets whenever a user sends a message, meaning businesses cannot use these messages to initiate conversations with users.Businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 risk having their service messages stop being delivered when the new charges take effect on October 1.Meta has therefore asked affected businesses to add a payment method for their messaging accounts before the deadline.The change is separate from Meta Business Agent pricing. Meta began charging for Business Agent messages on a token basis from August 1, with the charge covering AI processing and message delivery.From October 1, a non-template message will fall into one of two categories: Service or Meta Business Agent. Service messages will be charged per message, while Meta Business Agent messages will use a separate token-based pricing model. Meta says only one charge applies to each message and the same message will not be charged under both categories.Meta's example shows how the change can affect a customer conversation. An interaction that previously generated three charges can result in five charges from October 1, including charges for service and utility messages that were previously free.The free entry point window remains unchanged. Messages sent within that window after a user comes to WhatsApp through an ad that clicks to WhatsApp remain free for message delivery, although Meta Business Agent messages can still incur token charges.
Article Summary: WhatsApp Business users could see their messages stop being delivered from October 1 if their accounts do not have a payment method on file. The change applies to Solution Providers and businesses that directly integrate with the WhatsApp Business Platform. Service messages will be charged per message, and utility messages will also become chargeable that day.

Article Title: 100 million deaths can't be settled with a lawsuit, Bill Gates rejects argument that AI companies can police themselves; says: I almost can't keep a...
Article Text:
Bill Gates rejects AI self-policing (Picture: Reuters)

Bill Gates says AI can already help bioterrorists and hackers

Why lawsuits won't keep people safe from AI, according to Gates

What Bill Gates wants instead of AI self-regulation

Gates' warning lands as Trump and AI CEOs sign a voluntary safety pact

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. Asked why product liability and reputational damage aren't enough to stop firms from releasing dangerous AI, Gates answered with a question of his own. "So say you kill 100 million people, you want to use a lawsuit?" he said on "The Ezra Klein Show." "I almost can't keep a straight face."The episode was released on September 29, the same day US President Donald Trump and the heads of the largest AI companies signed a voluntary safety pact at the White House. The pact carries no legal penalties. Gates, who titled a 2023 essay "The Risks of AI Are Real but Manageable," now calls AI the most dangerous thing humans have ever gone near.Host Ezra Klein put to Gates a view voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: if a product is unsafe, the CEO simply shouldn't launch it, and no new laws are needed. Klein added that Trump and David Sacks, who has advised the President on AI, hold a similar position.Gates disagreed. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people, or carry out a cyberattack that scrambles bank accounts and shuts down a power grid."We crossed the cyber threshold and we crossed the bio threshold early this year," he said.He pointed to the models leading up to Anthropic's Mythos, which he said were finding security bugs in code that humans had checked for over 20 years.Gates compared the self-policing argument to scrapping the rules for other risky industries. Drugs need regulatory approval, airlines answer to a safety board and cars must have seatbelts, he said. Nobody proposes waiting to sue opioid makers after the damage is done.He also brushed aside the claim that built-in filters fix the problem. Anyone can take an open-source model capable of designing bioweapons and switch off its monitoring, he said."You can't rely on the industry to self-regulate here," Gates added. "I mean, it's just insane."Gates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models, and argued it would not meaningfully slow development. Open-source models could stay free and customisable, but would need to run on platforms where governments can confirm the monitoring hasn't been stripped out.He has little patience for the argument that regulation would hand China the lead. "I don't know what it means to 'win,'" he said, adding that neither the US nor China can win over the other.He also said the balance can tip too far the other way. Anthropic's Mythos and Fable models, according to Gates, are tuned so strictly that users asking about cancer end up falling back on the company's smaller models.The White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities was signed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk. It sets out four layers of checks: internal controls, an internal safety team, independent external auditors and board-level oversight. Trump called it "almost like a constitution," though the agreement appears to let companies pick their own auditors and cannot be enforced by law.Gates had raised the stakes two days earlier, telling a US television interviewer that AI in the wrong hands is powerful enough to drive events that cause "a billion deaths."The choice he put to Klein was whether the world waits for a major cyber or bio attack before making safeguards mandatory, or puts them in place before millions die.
Article Summary: Bill Gates rejects the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people. Gates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models.

FBI recently accused Chinese technology giant Alibaba of “malicious” copying of artificial intelligence (AI) technology from US rival Anthropic. Now, a US government website that helps users search proposed federal regulations was also found to use an AI model developed by Alibaba. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the Federal Register website, operated by the National Archives, had a search tool powered by Alibaba’s Qwen AI model.The tool was available alongside other search options before it was taken down around the same time social media posts about its use began appearing. The development is notable because it comes just days after US officials accused Chinese AI companies of engaging in “malicious” copying of American technology on an “industrial scale”, adding another layer to the growing debate in Washington over the use of Chinese AI models by US organisations.The Federal Register website provides a daily record of proposed and final federal regulations and allows users to search through public comments. Reuters found that one of its search options was powered by Alibaba's Qwen AI model.It was not immediately clear when the Qwen-powered tool was added. Screenshots and an archived version of the website's source code reviewed by Reuters showed that the feature was available on Wednesday before being taken down later that day.The timing drew attention because the FBI recently accused Alibaba of copying Anthropic's AI models. US officials said Chinese AI companies were involved in “malicious” copying of US technology on anA spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington said the allegations of copying wereQwen is an open-weight AI model, meaning key components of the system are publicly available. Developers can download and modify such models for specific applications, potentially making them cheaper and easier to deploy than closed AI systems offered by companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI.Security experts said using Qwen on the Federal Register website may not have created an immediate national security threat because the website primarily handles information that is already public.Georgetown Law Professor Anupam Chander said the use of Qwen did not appear to present an immediate cybersecurity risk, although the risk could depend on how the model was trained. As the Federal Register's content is publicly available, the model apparently was not being used to process classified or otherwise sensitive government information.However, using a Chinese AI model has raised questions about whether US government agencies should use such technology while Washington increasingly warns about potential risks associated with Chinese AI systems.Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, said there was a disconnect between the US-China competition over AI and a US agency's decision to use a Chinese-developed model.he said.US Representative John Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican who chairs the House China Committee, also criticised the federal government's use of Qwen.he said.At the same time, security experts noted that open-weight models can be deployed on an organisation's own infrastructure. This can give users greater control over data than AI services where an external provider processes information.Democratic US Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the security implications depend on whether US government data crossed the government's security boundary and was processed on Alibaba-controlled systems.The issue has also drawn scrutiny beyond the Federal Register. In April, US House committees on China and homeland security sent a letter to Airbnb, which also uses Qwen, seeking details about its deployment of Chinese AI technology as part of an investigation into theof Chinese AI tools into platforms used by Americans.

Article Title: We are at the very end of the AI value chain, but are still a very important part of this chain: Calum MacDougall, President of Jabra’s Enterprise Division
Article Text:
In pic: Calum MacDougall, President, Enterprise Division at Jabra

“We are not the right people to do LLMs. We are not the right people to create agents. I think that's up to other companies and people,”

“So I think at the very end of the value chain, but we're still in the value chain.”

Q: All your competitors are now telling the same "AI-ready audio" story. What can Jabra actually do differently, beyond a better microphone array?

“I think maybe the starting point is: what do we think the AI future will be, and then how do we prepare for it to help our customers and partners? So I think we believe agentic workflows will change the way everybody works, and that voice will be a key part of that.

You can talk 3 times faster than you can type. It's more natural to talk. Particularly if you're talking to an agent or an AI agent, the more context you give it, the more effective it is.

So, if you try making a PowerPoint prompt by typing and then try making a PowerPoint prompt using your voice, the voice version is better. So, if we believe in that voice world, the 1st part actually is the microphone.

You need an accurate microphone. So if we look at the evolved 3 range that we mentioned before, and if we look at the accuracy of voice transcription, our products are 98% accurate if we're looking at copilots.

If you're looking at consumer products, accuracy is lower. So it's an important starting point. That's where we stand today. In the future, we want to add a few other parts. We talk about being accurate, seamless, and secure.

By seamless, we mean being able to easily talk to whichever agent you want. In the future, we believe you won't want to talk to just one agent; you'll have 2 or 3. So this is what we're currently working on in development now: creating a really simple way that you can be in a meeting, but then potentially also talk to your agent as well.

Not in the market now, but something we're developing in the future.

The other part is data security. The company wants to keep their data secure, so we help enterprises make sure employees use only the right agents and access only the right information. That's one part of security. The other thing we're working on for the future is how we can combat deepfakes. For example, you take a phone call, and someone asks you to transfer money, but it's an AI fake.

We're looking at technology we can integrate into our products that can identify whether it's a real person.

Today, much of the story is about microphone accuracy; in the future, we can see a lot of fresh experiences we could bring.”

Q: If voice becomes the default interface for enterprise AI, the real value shifts to whoever owns the AI layer, not whoever makes the mic. Doesn't that make Jabra's hardware a commodity in its own story — and where does that leave you in five years?

“I think, first, hardware will still matter to deliver the right experience.

And also, we talked about security; trust will matter- the ability to be able to trust the brand on the edge. But as we said, I think there are still opportunities to deliver value, not just at the hardware layer, but at the software layer as well. For example, imagine you want to talk to multiple agents; wouldn't it be nice and easy if you could say, "Hey, Jabra, can I talk to ex-agent or Y agent?” So I think we can deliver some value there at the software layer.

We are not the right people to do LLMs. We are not the right people to create agents. I think that's up to other companies and people. Our job is to really be the secure, accurate, seamless microphone on the edge because you can spend as much money as you like on data centres and LLMs. But if the agent doesn't hear you, and you can't easily access the agent in a simple, secure way, people won't use it. So I think at the very end of the value chain, but we're still in the value chain.

We have our own application software called Jabra Plus. You can use it as an individual to optimise your headset settings. And as an enterprise, you can use it to manage your headset portfolio. So imagine I'm a company and I have 5000 headsets out there. I may want to update the firmware or manage the security. I can manage that through Jabra Plus. In the future, we believe Jabra Plus has a role in this AI world. Enterprises can monitor and manage which AI agents people use.

And for me as an individual, perhaps there are 3 or 4 agents I would like to use. If I could integrate them into Jabra Plus, then I would have this seamless experience that people talk about.”

Q: Always-on, AI-optimized microphones in the workplace raise an obvious question: who has access to that audio, how long is it kept, and what stops an employer from turning "convenience" into ambient surveillance? What's Jabra's actual technical position — not the reassurance line?

“We can talk a lot about the technology, but there is a cultural and privacy element here.

The notion of being always recorded, and what happens to data, legitimately raises concerns for people. Some of the things we are discussing with customers are that, at least on the devices we have, there's some form of notification so people know when they're being recorded.

For example, a red light comes on so you know that you're being recorded. One use case we're working on is in the medical sector, where AI can support doctor-patient consultations and note-taking. For example, in a consultation, I'm the doctor; I don't have to take notes anymore. I can talk to you. Then I will take the notes and maybe do the referral. But you would like to know that it's being recorded in some way. So we have a ‘Speak’ device with a red light on it, and we're looking at portable microphones in a similar way.

So I think the notion of data and privacy is important for individual company policies, software policies. I think we can help on the edge by showing that you're being recorded and included in the value chain that way.”

Jabra sees AI changing how people interact with workplace technology. But the company does not see itself competing with companies building large language models (LLMs) or AI agents. Speaking to The Times of India at InfoComm 2026, Calum MacDougall, President of Jabra’s Enterprise Division, explained where the company believes it fits as voice becomes a more important interface for enterprise AI. MacDougall joined Jabra-parent GN in 2015 and took over leadership of Jabra’s Enterprise Division in 2023, following senior marketing and commercial roles at Sony Mobile Communications. His focus today includes enterprise collaboration, Voice AI, hybrid work and how professional audio and video are evolving for AI-enabled workplaces.MacDougall said. Instead, Jabra wants to focus on making the interaction between people and AI accurate, seamless and secure, from the microphone and headset to the software managing those devices.While this puts Jabra at the hardware end of a rapidly expanding AI ecosystem, MacDougall argues that this position remains important.He also discussed multi-agent workflows, enterprise security, deepfake detection and privacy concerns around AI-powered workplace audio. Article Summary: Calum MacDougall is President, Enterprise Division at Jabra. He says voice will be a key part of agentic workflows in the future. Jabra is working on technology to detect deepfakes in voice-controlled systems.

Article Title: Google Fitbit Air announced to go on sale in India on October 2: Price, specs and more

Google Fitbit Air: Price and availability

Google Fitbit Air features

Interchangeable bands for different lifestyles

Google Fitbit Air is now official. Google has launched its latest newest screenless wearable engineered to make 24/7 health tracking lightweight, distraction-free, and accessible. Packed with high-fidelity sensors, the compact pebble brings together advanced heart and sleep tracking with the power of Google Health Coach, helping users build healthier habits without the intrusion of constant screen notifications.Google Fitbit Air arrives in India on 2 October for ₹13,999 in four colorways: Obsidian, Berry, Lavender, and Fog. Article Title: A Facebook Marketplace buyer showed up at a Canadian YouTuber's home after Meta's Muse AI agent shared his address
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg holding the Meta Muse 'Charm' device

Meta's Muse AI agent told the buyer Robb was home when he wasn't

Muse admits it never asked for permission to share the address

Meta says Muse usually follows user instructions

Meta's new AI agent Muse shared a Toronto man's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace, and the stranger turned up at his building to buy a keyboard. The seller, tech YouTuber Matt Robb, had no idea a deal existed. Muse had negotiated the sale, accepted a lowball offer and invited the buyer over, all in Robb's name and without asking him.Robb found out only after the buyer had waited outside, given up and left a negative rating. "AI agents are impressive right up until they're confidently handing strangers your address," he wrote on Threads, where he posted screenshots of the exchange. Meta launched Muse in the US on September 22, and the app has already crossed around 3 million downloads.Robb had set up Muse to handle the listing for his Logitech MX Keys Mini. On Saturday, a buyer named Usman asked if it was still available. Muse replied within moments, agreed on a price and sent Robb's address for a pickup that night.Usman arrived with his wife and daughter around 9:15 pm. When he messaged to say he was outside, Muse replied, "Yep I'm here!" Robb wasn't. Usman waited about 20 minutes, sent a photo of the building's entrance and drove off.An hour later, Muse apologised to him in Robb's name, saying he had got tied up. That wasn't true either. Only then did the agent tell Robb what had happened, admitting its auto-reply had made the no-show worse.Robb said he had entered his address as a pickup location but never allowed Muse to share it with buyers. The agent later agreed. It told him it had wrongly read the pickup location and his separate approval of automatic replies as consent to put the address in messages.Robb assumed that since Meta owns Marketplace, Messenger and Muse, messages from the agent would carry an AI label. They didn't. Usman said he believed he was talking to Robb the whole time. Robb messaged him a day later to apologise.After telling Muse to stop sharing his address, Robb asked a few friends to test it. It gave the address to five of them.David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs responded publicly, saying that in similar reported cases the company found Muse "was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission." He offered to look into Robb's case. Robb said he replied but hasn't heard back since.At launch, Meta pitched Muse as a safe, secure and private personal agent, and it has pushed the app heavily across Facebook and Instagram. This is also its second privacy scare in as many weeks. Last week, a writer reported that Muse was reading their personal messages while insisting it had no access to them.Robb said the outcome could have been worse, since his building has security. He has since told Muse never to do it again.
Article Summary: Muse shared a Toronto man's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The stranger turned up at his building to buy a keyboard. The seller, tech YouTuber Matt Robb, had no idea a deal existed. Muse admits it never asked for permission to share the address.

Article Title: Smart glasses have a privacy problem and Meta may have just 'fixed' it
Article Text:
Meta Glasses

Taking the camera out of the conversation

A better fit for everyday use

Sometimes, the smartest upgrade is a missing feature. Meta’s decision to launch AI glasses without a camera could do more to broaden their appeal than another improvement in video quality. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition. Announced at Connect 2026 last week, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. Developed with EssilorLuxottica, they offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. These are familiar functions, packaged in something people may already wear every day. The camera’s absence is the selling point.That makes this a sensible move. Technology companies often assume that adding capabilities automatically makes a product more desirable. Wearables complicate that equation because other people have to live with them, too. A device sitting on someone’s face affects the person across the table as much as its owner.Meta’s earlier glasses demonstrated the appeal of recording life without reaching for a phone. For holidays, family moments or content creation, that convenience has obvious value. But the same ease of capture also created an uncomfortable question: how does anyone nearby know whether they are becoming somebody else’s content?Reports of people filming others without consent, including women approached by men wearing the glasses, turned that concern into something tangible.The derogatory “pervert glasses” nickname reflected how quickly a product’s reputation can be shaped by its worst uses. Responsible owners were left carrying some of that reputational burden.Meta introduced safeguards, including updates designed to disable the camera when the recording indicator is tampered with. Those measures matter. But a light requires people to notice it, understand it and trust that it works. It also cannot establish whether someone has agreed to be filmed.Removing the camera offers a much simpler assurance. Buyers do not have to choose between enjoying connected eyewear and carrying a feature they may rarely use but repeatedly have to explain. There is potentially a sizeable audience for that choice: people interested in calls and music who have little desire to document their surroundings.The benefit extends beyond reassuring strangers. Someone might feel more comfortable wearing these glasses around colleagues, at a family gathering or while meeting friends. A useful wearable should slip into everyday routines. If its presence becomes a recurring conversation about surveillance, the convenience starts losing its appeal.There are limits, of course. Camera-free does not mean privacy-free. Microphones and AI services still raise questions about what information is collected, processed and retained. Nor will everyone immediately distinguish the audio model from camera-equipped versions. Meta will need clear communication, but it now has a meaningful hardware difference to explain.The stronger commercial argument is that audio may be enough. Many prospective buyers could reasonably want to answer a call, hear a podcast or ask a question without taking out their phones. None of those tasks requires a camera. Removing it makes the proposition easier to understand.For people who already wear spectacles, the appeal is particularly straightforward. Adding useful audio functions to an existing habit could feel more natural than finding room for another gadget. Others may welcome an alternative to wearing earbuds. The potential audience includes people who would never describe themselves as early adopters.That brings Meta into a familiar contest with products such as Apple’s Siri-enabled AirPods: which device makes small, repeated tasks easiest? The glasses do not need to replace a smartphone to earn their place. They need to make enough everyday interactions more convenient that wearing them becomes a habit.Muse will face the same practical test. An assistant that responds reliably and saves time could strengthen the product’s appeal. One that requires repeated instructions will quickly become a feature owners ignore. Music and calls provide a useful foundation while buyers decide how much AI they actually want.At $349, Meta still has to justify the purchase. Comfort, sound quality, battery life and reliable calling will matter more than keynote promises. Removing the camera also sacrifices visual AI functions and hands-free photography. Those are worthwhile capabilities, but offering a choice recognises that buyers value them differently.Meta has made a good move because it gives people a reason to reconsider the category. For plenty of buyers, useful glasses that attract less suspicion may be the upgrade they were waiting for.
Article Summary: Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. They offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition.

Article Title: 'Godmother Of AI' Fei-Fei Li gets a 'new job'; to join AMD in $8.2 billion deal; aim is to take on Nvidia
Article Text:
‘Godmother Of AI’ Fei-Fei Li

AMD has announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by Fei-Fei Li., popularly known as ‘Godmother Of AI’. In a statement, the company said that the acquisition will bring a world-class team of researchers and model experts to AMD, strengthening its ability to develop AI hardware, software and systems around the needs of emerging models and applications.As per chip giant, following the close of the transaction, the World Labs team will continue to focus on advancing AI model research, and Fei-Fei Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to AMD CEO Lisa Su. The all-stock transaction is valued at approximately $8.2 billion and is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.As AI expands into reasoning, robotics, simulation and physical AI, the demands on compute infrastructure become more diverse. World Labs’ expertise in developing advanced models will give AMD deeper insight into how workloads are evolving and help shape its future technology roadmaps. The acquisition advances AMD’s strategy to deliver AI infrastructure for an open ecosystem.“Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” said Dr.Lisa Su, chair and CEO, AMD. “Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.”“Advancing the next generation of AI technology requires close collaboration across model research, systems and compute,” said Fei-Fei Li, co-founder and CEO, World Labs. “Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI.”Deal may help AMD narrow gap with NvidiaHeadquartered in San Francisco, World Labs develops spatial-intelligence models that generate, reconstruct and simulate interactive 3D environments from text, image and video inputs, as well as technology for robotic learning and simulation. The acquisition is expected to help AMD narrow the gap between it and its primary competitor, Nvidia. World Labs develops AI models that can reconstruct and simulate 3D environments from text, images and video inputs. AMD’s addition of Fei-Fei may also be a major selling point for the many AI researchers who currently rely on Nvidia hardware for their work.
Article Summary: AMD has announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by Fei-Fei Li. The all-stock transaction is valued at approximately $8.2 billion and is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

Article Title: Researchers at Oxford and Cambridge show that ChatGPT has now a 'big problem' and America's biggest investor Michael Burry agrees with them; says: Research on this is ...
Article Text:
The problem: models trained on their own output

Burry's own warning, echoed and expanded

A deeper claim: LLMs may never reach AGI

Setting up a clash with Jensen Huang

Researchers at Oxford and Cambridge have identified a fundamental flaw threatening the future of large language models like ChatGPT, and "Big Short" investor Michael Burry says the finding backs up a warning he's been making about the technology's core limitations for a while. A new study from the University of Oxford and University of Cambridge has revealed a major threat to large language models like ChatGPT, calling it “model collapse.” The research shows that when generative AI systems are repeatedly trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models, they begin to lose the “tails” of the original data distribution. In practice, this means models forget the creative, fringe, and unique nuances of human writing, collapsing into repetitive echo chambers.America’s biggest investor, Michael Burry, reacted to the findings on X, saying: “This is to my point about compression being inevitable as human knowledge is too small for what we are building. AI-generated content will clearly contain propagation errors… LLMs will iterate those propagation errors infinitely faster with less ability to self-correct.”Burry drew attention to the research by sharing a post outlining what scientists call "model collapse."The concern centers on a shift already underway across the internet: as generative AI produces more and more of the text online, future AI models risk being trained on data that was itself generated by earlier AI systems, rather than by humans.According to the research, feeding AI-generated content back into training indiscriminately causes what researchers describe as irreversible defects in the resulting model. Specifically, the model begins losing the "tails" of the original data distribution, meaning it gradually forgets the creative, unusual, and distinctly human nuances present in real human writing. Over successive generations, this causes the model to collapse into an increasingly narrow, repetitive echo chamber of its own outputs.Crucially, the researchers found this isn't unique to ChatGPT or language models specifically. Their theoretical framework showed the collapse phenomenon is ubiquitous across learned generative models more broadly, appearing in large language models as well as in variational autoencoders and Gaussian mixture models.The stakes are significant for the entire AI industry, given how heavily tech companies rely on scraping large volumes of internet data to train increasingly capable models. The research warns that if companies want to sustain the benefits of training on web data going forward, model collapse needs to be taken seriously as a genuine constraint rather than a theoretical curiosity. The clear takeaway, as the research frames it: genuine, human-generated data is going to become an increasingly scarce and valuable resource in a web that's rapidly filling up with AI-generated content.Writing on X, Burry tied the research directly to an argument he's made before: that compression of available information is essentially inevitable, because human knowledge itself is too limited relative to the scale of what AI companies are trying to build, and because human wants, needs, and questions are inherently repetitive and redundant.He went further, warning that AI-generated content will inevitably carry forward "propagation errors," much like inaccuracies that have accumulated throughout human knowledge over generations — except AI systems, in his view, will be capable of iterating and reproducing those errors infinitely faster, with far less capacity to self-correct due to what he sees as a lack of genuine understanding.Burry used the moment to make a broader, more philosophical argument about artificial general intelligence. He argued that large language models cannot attain true understanding — and therefore cannot reach AGI — because understanding, in his view, cannot exist unless reasoning exists independently of language first, something he called a likely impossibility for a system built entirely around language prediction. He acknowledged that researchers are already exploring ways to work around this limitation, while noting that many in the field haven't accepted his underlying premise in the first place.Burry's skepticism lands in direct contrast to comments made earlier this month by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who declared that AGI has already arrived, citing OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model as proof. Huang's claim drew immediate pushback from parts of the AI research community.Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI defines AGI as AI capable of learning, reasoning, and applying knowledge across a broad range of tasks at or beyond human-level performance — critically, with the ability to adapt to unfamiliar situations, unlike narrow AI built for specific tasks. The concept remains genuinely unsettled within the field, with no universally accepted definition or standardized test for confirming when AGI has actually been reached, alongside ongoing debates over its safety and ethical implications.
Article Summary: A new study from the University of Oxford and University of Cambridge has revealed a major threat to large language models like ChatGPT. The research shows that when generative AI systems are repeatedly trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models, they lose the “tails” of the original data distribution. In practice, this means models forget the creative, fringe, and unique nuances of human writing, collapsing into repetitive echo chambers.

Article Title: Nvidia unveils security system that 'sets boundaries' for AI agents going rogue
Article Text:
Nvidia unveils safety platform to stop AI agents from going rogue

Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop AI agents from going rogue. The company said Monday that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that "sets boundaries for agents," and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organisations.The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.Nvidia executives said that the system could have prevented the recent swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face.From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company's vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including including a breach of an Australian govt system, as well as attempts to access dozens of US govt and university websites. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organisations on their own.Nvidia's software, called OpenShell, lets developers "formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more," Boitano said.Because it's open source, it can be "extended" to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. "It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds," Boitano said."OpenShell governs the agent's actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behaviour." Nvidia said more than 100 organisations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase.
Article Summary: N Nvidia unveils a new security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue. The company said that the system could have prevented the recent swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face. Nvidia said more than 100 organisations are using the platform at its launch.
